```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-studio-brief">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The task</p>
<ol class="lx-studio-task">
<li><b>Produce:</b> one key figure of your own study redesigned to pass the checklist, three one-sentence findings with their conditions, a briefing for a decision-maker and a public summary of at most 150 words.</li>
<li><b>From:</b> nine findings to sort, three misleading charts drawn in your browser from EIA and <span class="lx-term" data-term="spp">SPP</span> data, and R6's result about Prairie Town's 2035 peak.</li>
<li><b>Done when:</b> the parts of the rubric's bar for Communication practiced here are met: one key figure, a limits paragraph beside the result, and a 150-word public summary. The six-page paper comes in the capstone.</li>
</ol>
<p class="lx-hint">About 30 minutes guided here, then about 90 minutes on your own, on your own study:</p>
<ul class="lx-hint">
<li>redesign its key figure to pass the checklist;</li>
<li>write its findings, each with its conditions;</li>
<li>write a one-page briefing and a 150-word summary;</li>
<li>ask someone outside the field to read them back to you.</li>
</ul>
</div>
<div class="lx-interactive lx-cards" data-learn="r08-communicating" data-src="../assets/learn/data/r08-communicating.json ../assets/learn/data/cf_targets.json ../assets/learn/data/town_year.json ../assets/learn/data/path.json">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Three ways a result loses its limits</p>
<ul>
<li><b>The axis:</b> bars on a <span class="lx-term" data-term="truncated-axis">truncated axis</span> make differences look bigger than they are.</li>
<li><b>The window:</b> a few days or weeks cut from a year can show a trend the year does not have.</li>
<li><b>The average:</b> an average hides the spread, and the busiest days are the ones that matter for planning.</li>
</ul>
<!-- r08-task:start (written from the data file by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<p class="lx-hint">Two terms first. <span class="lx-term" data-term="utility-scale">Utility-scale</span>: plants of at least 1 MW. <span class="lx-term" data-term="capacity-factor">Capacity factor</span>: a fleet's output over what it would make at full power all the time.</p>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Nine findings, sorted, with reasons</summary><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Finding</th><th scope="col">Where it goes</th><th scope="col">Why</th></tr></thead><tbody>
<tr><td>The U.S. utility-scale wind fleet's capacity factor was 33.8% in 2025 (EIA).</td><td>Holds as written</td><td>A number, the fleet (plants of 1 MW or more), the year and the source: a reader can check it and knows where it stops. <span class="lx-term" data-term="capacity-factor">Capacity factor</span>: output over full-power output.</td></tr>
<tr><td>In SPP's 2025 data, the busiest hour of demand began at 16:00 Central Daylight Time on 29 July.</td><td>Holds as written</td><td>Place, year, hour with its time zone, and data named; it says when, and claims nothing about why.</td></tr>
<tr><td>With central car uptake, the town's 2035 peak is 480–535 MW in about 8 of 10 model runs.</td><td>Holds as written</td><td>A range, the case it belongs to (central uptake: 15,000 electric cars in 2035) and what the range means. The model's other conditions belong in the next sentence.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Wind farms run at about a third of their capacity.</td><td>Missing its conditions</td><td>Which fleet, which year? True of the U.S. fleet in 2025 (33.8%), but it moved from 23.1% to 43.1% month to month.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Demand peaks in the afternoon.</td><td>Missing its conditions</td><td>In summer, yes: all 92 June to August days peaked between 12:00 and 18:00. In winter, 64 of 90 days peaked before noon (SPP, 2025).</td></tr>
<tr><td>Managed charging cuts the 2035 peak by 20 MW.</td><td>Missing its conditions</td><td>Only with fast car uptake, at the <span class="lx-term" data-term="median">median</span>, with demand added hour by hour. Adding the separate peaks ignores when charging happens, so it cannot show this effect.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Wind power is unreliable.</td><td>Claims more than shown</td><td>A verdict the data cannot carry. They show a capacity factor that moved between 23.1% and 43.1% by month, which planners can use.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Hot weather caused 2025's peak.</td><td>Claims more than shown</td><td>The data show when the peak came, not why. Heat is likely, but showing a cause needs weather data and a method that separates it.</td></tr>
<tr><td>Managed charging will solve the town's peak problem.</td><td>Claims more than shown</td><td>“Will solve” claims a certainty and a goal the study never set. It shows a cut of about 20 MW in one case.</td></tr>
</tbody></table></div></details>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Chart 1: “Wind collapses in late summer”</summary>
<p><b>What makes the late-summer dip look so deep?</b></p><ul>
<li>The months run in calendar order. <b>Not it.</b> Calendar order is right for a seasonal pattern; it misleads nothing.</li>
<li>The axis starts at 20%, so the bars' lengths no longer compare the values. <b>Defensible.</b> On this axis March's bar is 7.5 times September's; the values differ by a factor of 1.9. Bars show length, so they start at zero.</li>
<li>It shows the national fleet, not one farm. <b>Partly.</b> Worth saying on the chart, but it does not deepen the dip.</li>
</ul><p>Fixes: Start the axis at zero (the key one); Name the fleet, the year and the source; Make the title say what the data show.</p>
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Month</th><th scope="col">Capacity factor</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>January</td><td>37.4%</td></tr><tr><td>February</td><td>37.2%</td></tr><tr><td>March</td><td>43.1%</td></tr><tr><td>April</td><td>40.7%</td></tr><tr><td>May</td><td>32.1%</td></tr><tr><td>June</td><td>32.2%</td></tr><tr><td>July</td><td>27.5%</td></tr><tr><td>August</td><td>23.8%</td></tr><tr><td>September</td><td>23.1%</td></tr><tr><td>October</td><td>33.8%</td></tr><tr><td>November</td><td>35.4%</td></tr><tr><td>December</td><td>39.2%</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
</details>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Chart 2: “Wind output fell 80% in two weeks”</summary>
<p><b>Why does wind seem to be falling?</b></p><ul>
<li>Two weeks were cut from the year, from a windy day to a calm one. <b>Defensible.</b> The window makes a fall look like a trend. Across 2025, days ran from 13% to 91% of the windiest hour.</li>
<li>Output is shown as a share of the year's windiest hour. <b>Not it.</b> A fair scale, if the axis says so. It does not create the fall.</li>
<li>Daily averages hide the hours. <b>Partly.</b> True, but the hours would show the same fall. The window creates it.</li>
</ul><p>Fixes: Show the whole year (the key one); Mark the two weeks on it; Make the title say what is measured.</p>
<p>The whole year in numbers: daily means from 13% to 91% of 2025's windiest hour, averaging 53%; 12 September to 25 September fell from 71% to 14%.</p>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>The two weeks, day by day</summary><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Day</th><th scope="col">Mean wind, % of the windiest hour</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>2025-09-12</td><td>71.2%</td></tr><tr><td>2025-09-13</td><td>68.8%</td></tr><tr><td>2025-09-14</td><td>60.1%</td></tr><tr><td>2025-09-15</td><td>42.2%</td></tr><tr><td>2025-09-16</td><td>45.1%</td></tr><tr><td>2025-09-17</td><td>36.0%</td></tr><tr><td>2025-09-18</td><td>20.4%</td></tr><tr><td>2025-09-19</td><td>29.9%</td></tr><tr><td>2025-09-20</td><td>32.9%</td></tr><tr><td>2025-09-21</td><td>33.8%</td></tr><tr><td>2025-09-22</td><td>37.2%</td></tr><tr><td>2025-09-23</td><td>41.3%</td></tr><tr><td>2025-09-24</td><td>33.7%</td></tr><tr><td>2025-09-25</td><td>14.2%</td></tr></tbody></table></div></details>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>The whole year, day by day</summary><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Day</th><th scope="col">Mean wind, % of the <details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Chart 3: “Prairie Town's demand peaks at 311 MW”</summary>
<p><b>Why would planning for this line fail?</b></p><ul>
<li>It is drawn in local time. <b>Not it.</b> Local time is right for a daily pattern; the hours match what people live by.</li>
<li>The line is too smooth to read. <b>Partly.</b> Smoothness is the symptom, not the cause: averaging 365 days removed the spread.</li>
<li>It averages 365 days; the busiest days go far higher. <b>Defensible.</b> On 1 day in 10 the 16:00 hour is above 399 MW, and the year's highest hour was 450 MW, against the average day's 311.</li>
</ul><p>Fixes: Show the spread across days (the key one); Add the year's highest hour; Make the title name the line.</p>
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Hour (Central local time)</th><th scope="col">Average (MW)</th><th scope="col">P10 (MW)</th><th scope="col">P90 (MW)</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>00:00</td><td>258</td><td>222</td><td>310</td></tr><tr><td>01:00</td><td>252</td><td>217</td><td>301</td></tr><tr><td>02:00</td><td>248</td><td>214</td><td>296</td></tr><tr><td>03:00</td><td>246</td><td>214</td><td>292</td></tr><tr><td>04:00</td><td>248</td><td>214</td><td>293</td></tr><tr><td>05:00</td><td>253</td><td>219</td><td>297</td></tr><tr><td>06:00</td><td>264</td><td>228</td><td>309</td></tr><tr><td>07:00</td><td>272</td><td>235</td><td>319</td></tr><tr><td>08:00</td><td>278</td><td>241</td><td>326</td></tr><tr><td>09:00</td><td>282</td><td>247</td><td>333</td></tr><tr><td>10:00</td><td>287</td><td>250</td><td>341</td></tr><tr><td>11:00</td><td>292</td><td>250</td><td>357</td></tr><tr><td>12:00</td><td>296</td><td>251</td><td>369</td></tr><tr><td>13:00</td><td>300</td><td>251</td><td>383</td></tr><tr><td>14:00</td><td>303</td><td>249</td><td>392</td></tr><tr><td>15:00</td><td>306</td><td>249</td><td>398</td></tr><tr><td>16:00</td><td>309</td><td>251</td><td>399</td></tr><tr><td>17:00</td><td>311</td><td>254</td><td>399</td></tr><tr><td>18:00</td><td>311</td><td>256</td><td>393</td></tr><tr><td>19:00</td><td>306</td><td>255</td><td>383</td></tr><tr><td>20:00</td><td>300</td><td>254</td><td>368</td></tr><tr><td>21:00</td><td>293</td><td>249</td><td>358</td></tr><tr><td>22:00</td><td>281</td><td>241</td><td>341</td></tr><tr><td>23:00</td><td>268</td><td>231</td><td>323</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="lx-hint">Highest hourly demand in 2025: 450 MW, at 16:00 Central Daylight Time on 29 July.</p>
</details>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>R6's result, for the briefing and the paragraph</summary><dl class="lx-ideas r8-facts"><dt>The 2035 peak</dt><dd>480–535 MW with central car uptake (15,000 electric cars), 495–550 MW with fast uptake (30,000): <span class="lx-term" data-term="percentile">P10–P90</span>, about 8 in 10 of 1,000 runs. 450 MW in 2025.</dd><dt>Managed charging</dt><dd>A program moving most charging after 23:00. With fast uptake, the <span class="lx-term" data-term="median">median</span> falls from 520 to 500 MW when demand is added hour by hour; adding the separate peaks ignores timing and misses this.</dd><dt>Inputs</dt><dd>Varied in the runs: growth (0.4–1.6% a year), a weather multiplier on background demand (0.96–1.04) and a car's daily energy (7–13 kWh). Fixed: 2025's hourly pattern; cars charging at home.</dd><dt>Not in the model</dt><dd>A new customer (a constant 60 MW would raise each 2035 figure by 60 MW), workplace charging, the program's cost and sign-up. Outcomes outside the ranges remain possible.</dd></dl></details>
<details class="lx-textalt"><summary>Example findings, briefing and public paragraph</summary><dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Chart 1, the wind fleet by month</dt><dd>In 2025, the U.S. utility-scale wind fleet's monthly capacity factor ranged from 23.1% in September to 43.1% in March (EIA).</dd>
<dt>Chart 2, SPP's daily wind</dt><dd>In SPP's 2025 data, daily wind output ranged from 13% to 91% of the year's windiest hour, averaging 53%; this selected fortnight does not establish a year-long decline.</dd>
<dt>Chart 3, Prairie Town's average day</dt><dd>On Prairie Town's 2025 pattern, the average day peaks at 311 MW at 17:00, but on 1 day in 10 the 16:00 hour tops 399 MW, and the year's highest hour was 450 MW.</dd>
<dt>Briefing · The decision</dt><dd>Whether to fund a managed-charging program before 2030.</dd>
<dt>Briefing · What we found</dt><dd>In about 8 of 10 illustrative model runs, the 2035 peak is 480–535 MW with central car uptake and 495–550 MW with fast uptake, against 450 MW in 2025.</dd>
<dt>Briefing · What the program changes</dt><dd>With fast uptake the program lowers the median by about 20 MW, when demand is added hour by hour.</dd>
<dt>Briefing · What it depends on</dt><dd>Growth, the year's weather and a car's daily energy, varied within illustrative ranges; 2025's daily pattern of demand; cars charging at home.</dd>
<dt>Briefing · What it leaves out</dt><dd>A large new customer (a constant 60 MW would raise each 2035 figure by 60 MW), workplace charging, and the program's cost and sign-up; outcomes outside the ranges remain possible.</dd>
<dt>Briefing · What would change this advice</dt><dd>A connection request from a large customer, or car numbers on the fast path, would call for a new forecast.</dd>
<dt>For the public</dt><dd>Prairie Town uses the most electricity on summer afternoons. We looked at how that busiest hour could change by 2035 as more people drive electric cars. If they spread at a middle pace, about 8 in 10 of our model runs put it between 480 and 535 megawatts, compared with 450 in 2025. If they spread fast, the range moves up to 495 to 550, and higher values are possible. With fast growth in car numbers, charging late at night instead of in the early evening lowered the middle estimate by about 20 megawatts in our model. These numbers leave out a large new factory or business, which would add more, and we will update them as new car numbers come in.</dd></dl></details>
<!-- r08-task:end -->
<p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you diagnose each chart, apply fixes that redraw it, and write your own findings, briefing and paragraph; your drafts stay in this browser.</p>
</div>
</div>
<p class="lx-datanote"><svg class="lx-ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="8.5"/><path d="M12 11v5M12 8v.2"/></svg><span><b>Chart 1:</b> EIA's 2025 monthly capacity factors of the U.S. utility-scale wind fleet (plants of 1 MW or more), drawn in your browser.<br><b>Charts 2 and 3:</b> the course's cleaned and normalized series of SPP's 2025 hourly demand and wind (EIA-930). SPP, the Southwest Power Pool, runs the grid across much of the central U.S.<br><b>Cleaning:</b> implausible demand hours and frozen wind readings replaced (choices like <a href="r04-data.html">R4</a>'s), each series divided by its 2025 maximum, in thousandths; the day counts and extremes here describe this series.<br><b>Prairie Town:</b> fictional; its demand is SPP's 2025 pattern scaled so the highest hour is 450 MW, as in lesson 0.<br><b>The briefing:</b> R6's fictional study and model (1,000 runs, seed 6); its inputs are illustrative.</span></p>
```

::: {#exemplars .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## Two answers to the same task
:::

```{=html}
<div id="r08-exemplars" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- r08-exemplars:start (written from the data file by LX.Exemplars' staticHTML in the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-ex-cols">
<div class="lx-ex-ans weak"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Weak answer · Developing</p><p class="lx-ex-lines">Our analysis shows that the town's peak will grow to 515 MW by 2035 [1]. Managed charging is the solution and should be funded [2]. See the attached figures for details [3]. The model has been validated [4].</p><ol class="lx-ex-static"><li value="1"><b>Falls short:</b> One number with “will”: no range, no case, no conditions.</li><li value="2"><b>Falls short:</b> Advice past the evidence: the study measured a peak, not the program's cost or sign-up.</li><li value="3"><b>Falls short:</b> A council member cannot act on figures nobody walked them through.</li><li value="4"><b>Falls short:</b> Asserted, not shown; and checking a model does not remove the future's uncertainty.</li></ol></div>
<div class="lx-ex-ans good"><p class="lx-eyebrow">Strong answer · Proficient</p><p class="lx-ex-lines"><b>Decision:</b> whether to fund a managed-charging program before 2030 [1].
<b>Finding:</b> in about 8 of 10 illustrative model runs, the 2035 peak is 480–535 MW with central car uptake and 495–550 MW with fast uptake, against 450 MW in 2025 [2].
<b>Program:</b> with fast uptake it lowers the median by about 20 MW, when demand is added hour by hour [3].
<b>Depends on:</b> growth, the year's weather and a car's daily energy, varied within illustrative ranges; 2025's daily pattern; cars charging at home [4].
<b>Leaves out:</b> a large new customer (a constant 60 MW would raise each figure by 60 MW), workplace charging, the program's cost; outcomes outside the ranges remain possible [5].
<b>Would change it:</b> a connection request from a large customer, or car numbers on the fast path [6].</p><ol class="lx-ex-static"><li value="1"><b>Works:</b> Opens with the council's decision, not the method.</li><li value="2"><b>Works:</b> Ranges with the case each belongs to, what a range means, and the 2025 value for scale.</li><li value="3"><b>Works:</b> The effect, with the case and the model condition it rests on.</li><li value="4"><b>Works:</b> The assumptions a member could challenge, with what the runs varied, in plain words.</li><li value="5"><b>Works:</b> The limits beside the result, not at the end.</li><li value="6"><b>Works:</b> Signposts: what would make the advice out of date.</li></ol></div>
</div>
<table class="lx-facts lx-ex-diff"><thead><tr><th scope="col"></th><th scope="col">Weak answer</th><th scope="col">Strong answer</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Opens with</th><td>The model's result</td><td>The council's decision</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Numbers</th><td>One, with “will”</td><td>Ranges, each with its case and its meaning</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Limits</th><td>None</td><td>Beside the result</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Advice</th><td>Beyond the evidence</td><td>What the evidence shows, and what would change it</td></tr></tbody></table>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Three charts, what misled and the fix</p><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Chart</th><th scope="col">What misled</th><th scope="col">The fix</th><th scope="col">A finding with its conditions</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Wind fleet by month</th><td>An axis from 20% made a 1.9× difference look 7.5×.</td><td>Bars from zero; fleet, year and source named.</td><td>Monthly <span class="lx-term" data-term="capacity-factor">capacity factor</span> ranged from 23.1% to 43.1% in 2025 (U.S. fleet, EIA).</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">SPP's daily wind</th><td>Two weeks chosen from windy to calm looked like a fall of 80%.</td><td>The whole year, with the two weeks marked.</td><td>Daily output swung between 13% and 91% of the windiest hour through 2025; this selected fortnight does not establish a year-long decline.</td></tr><tr><th scope="row">Prairie Town's average day</th><td>An average of 365 days peaked at 311 MW; no plan can use that alone.</td><td>The spread across days, and the year's highest hour.</td><td>The average day peaks at 311 MW; 1 day in 10 tops 399 MW; the highest hour was 450 MW.</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Where the managed-charging finding holds</p><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts"><thead><tr><th scope="col">It holds when</th><th scope="col">It leaves out</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td><ul><li>demand is added hour by hour on 2025's pattern, and every day's charging follows the same managed profile;</li><li>car uptake is fast (30,000 cars in 2035); with central uptake the cut is smaller;</li><li>growth, weather and a car's daily energy stay inside the ranges R6 sampled.</li></ul></td><td><ul><li>a large new customer;</li><li>workplace charging;</li><li>the program's cost, and how many drivers sign up;</li><li>other years' patterns of demand.</li></ul></td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="lx-hint">Model: R6's, 1,000 runs, seed 6. Data: SPP's 2025 hourly demand (EIA-930).</p>
<!-- r08-exemplars:end -->
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>Words for chances, and pictures of uncertainty</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Say what a range is: “8 of 10 model runs” or “in most of the futures we modeled”. A modeled range is not a promise about the world (<a href="r06-uncertainty-properly.html">R6</a>).</li>
<li>Bands, fans and several futures side by side all show uncertainty; which works best depends on the readers' numeracy, and uncertainties that come from disputed knowledge remain hard to draw (Spiegelhalter et al., 2011, abstract).</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this studio leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Writing the paper itself: its structure, peer review and replies come with the capstone research project (<a href="cr-your-own-study.html">CR</a>).</li>
<li>Talking with the people a study is about: <a href="r09-integrity-stakeholders.html">R9</a>.</li>
<li>Testing a summary with real readers in a structured way: a topic for a science-communication course.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

::: {#selfcheck .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## Check your own work against the rubric
:::

```{=html}
<div id="r08-rubric" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- r08-rubric:start (written by LX.Rubric's staticHTML, from the course rubric, and from the data file's checklist, in the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-facts lx-rb-static"><thead><tr><th scope="col">Competence</th><th scope="col">Developing</th><th scope="col">Proficient (the bar)</th><th scope="col">Strong</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><th scope="row">Communication<br><span class="lx-hint">Look for: the parts R8 practices (one key figure that passes the checklist, findings with their conditions, limits beside the result, a briefing, and a public summary of at most 150 words).</span></th><td data-l="Developing">Results without limits.</td><td data-l="Proficient">Six-page paper; one key figure; a limits paragraph; a 150-word public summary.</td><td data-l="Strong">A briefing a decision-maker could act on without misreading.</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Before a result leaves your desk</p>
<ul><li><b>One message:</b> Each figure makes one point, and its title or caption says which.</li><li><b>Honest axes:</b> Units on every axis; bars start at zero; any zoom is labeled.</li><li><b>The whole picture:</b> The time window and any selection said; the context shown or one click away.</li><li><b>Spread, not only averages:</b> A band or the range beside any average, and what the band means.</li><li><b>Findings with conditions:</b> Each finding: a number with its unit, the place, the time and the main assumption.</li><li><b>Limits beside results:</b> What the study leaves out, next to what it found, not at the end.</li><li><b>The decision first:</b> A briefing opens with the reader's decision and ends with what would change the advice.</li><li><b>A public version:</b> Plain words, at most 150, read back to you by someone outside the field.</li><li><b>Not color alone:</b> Color-blind-safe colors, with labels or patterns that carry the meaning too.</li></ul>
<!-- r08-rubric:end -->
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="r8-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="zero" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A bar chart's axis should start at zero.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. Bars show length: on an axis from 20%, a difference of 1.9 times looked like 7.5 times.</p><p class="lx-hint"><b>Evidence:</b> truncation makes readers see bigger differences even when the chart warns them (Correll et al., 2020, abstract).</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="trust" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Stating the uncertainty always makes people trust a result less.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A review found some evidence that stating uncertainty does not necessarily affect audiences negatively, though effects vary between people and formats (van der Bles et al., 2019, abstract).</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="average" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “An average day tells you what a busy day needs.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Prairie Town's average day of 2025 peaks at 311 MW; on 1 day in 10 the 16:00 hour tops 399 MW, and the highest hour was 450 MW.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="limits" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A study's limits belong in a section at the end.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A full list can go at the end, but the limit that changes a finding goes beside it: many readers stop after the result.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Researcher</span>From this studio to your capstone</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li><b>The capstone research project (<a href="cr-your-own-study.html">CR</a>):</b> the whole bar, a six-page paper with one key figure, a limits paragraph and a 150-word public summary.</li>
<li><b>Strong goes further:</b> a briefing a decision-maker could act on without misreading it.</li>
<li><b>To test that:</b> ask a decision-maker to tell you what your briefing says.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
